AKBL.summary: Askari Bank scores 80.6/100, driven mainly by fast growth (sales up 26.8% a year and EPS up 17.5% a year over three years), a 7.3% dividend yield paid in each of the last three fiscal years on record, and a share price above its 200-day average. BOP.summary: Bank of Punjab scores 79.5/100, mainly because it looks cheap (P/E 5.5 against a sector median of 6.7), pays a high dividend (10.2% yield, paid in each of the last 3 years on record) and has grown sales and earnings strongly. strengths: Cheap on earnings: P/E of 6.1, about 9% below the sector median of 6.7
Dividend yield of 9.4%, with cash dividends paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years and four 40% cash payouts announced in 2026
EPS grew about 18.4% a year over 3 years and net margin rose from 9.84% to 11.83%

AICL.summary: Adamjee Insurance scores 74.7/100 (HOLD), helped mainly by strong earnings growth (EPS up about 25.7% a year over three years), a low P/E of 5.4 (slightly below the sector median of 5.8), and a 5.3% dividend yield with cash paid in every year on record. Held back by a price below its 200-day average and a small lag versus the KSE-100. Two factors, revenue growth and price-to-book, could not be scored because data is missing, so about a third of the picture is unseen (67.6% coverage).
strengths: EPS rose from Rs 7.39 in 2022 to Rs 14.66 in 2025, and profit after tax roughly doubled over that period.
Valuation looks modest: P/E 5.4 versus a sector median of 5.8.
Consistent cash dividends, with a 5.3% yield and recent payouts of 30% and 20% of face value.
risks: Net margin slipped to 12.98% in 2025 from 15.01% in 2024 and 15.22% in 2022, so profit growth is not coming from better margins.
Weak price trend: below the 200-day average and about 4 points behind the KSE-100 over a year.
The scorecard cannot see sales, equity/book value, debt, solvency or cash flow, which matter for an insurer; the low P/E could reflect earnings the market doubts will last.
checks: Find the insurance revenue and underwriting result in the annual report to see whether profit comes from core insurance or from investment income.
Check equity and book value to judge price-to-book, plus the solvency and capital position against regulatory requirements.
Read the quarterly results for the period ended 30 September 2026 to see whether the 2025 earnings level and margins are holding.

IMAGE.summary: Image Pakistan scores 74.6/100 (HOLD), driven by strong sales and margin growth and a P/E of 9.2 that is below the sector median of 12.3. Only 62% of the data is covered, because debt, liquidity, cash flow and working capital could not be scored.

Cash dividends paid in each of the last 2 fiscal years, with a 3.9% yield

HCAR.summary: Honda Atlas Cars scores 72.7 out of 100 (HOLD), mainly because the shares look cheap: a P/E of 6.0 against a sector median of 7.6, plus a 3.7% dividend yield and a big rise in earnings from a very low base. The weak spot is the share price, which is below its 200-day average and about 40 points behind the KSE-100 over a year. The score also rests on only 62% of the data, because debt, liquidity and cash flow could not be assessed.
strengths: Valuation: P/E of 6.0 is about 22% below the sector median of 7.6.
Profit recovery: EPS rose from Rs 1.82 in 2023 to Rs 22.64 in 2026, and profit after tax reached about Rs 3.2 billion.
Cash dividends of 80% and then 90% of face value were announced in May 2025 and May 2026, giving a 3.7% yield.
risks: The 100/100 earnings and profitability scores flatter the picture: they measure from a very weak 2023 base. Net margin has fallen each year since 2024, from 4.24% to 3.47% to 2.64%.
Sales are volatile, falling from Rs 95.1 billion in 2023 to Rs 55.1 billion in 2024 before reaching Rs 122.3 billion in 2026. The 8.7% annual growth figure hides that swing.
The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash conversion or cash flow, which together carry 38% of the weight. The company's borrowing and its ability to turn profit into cash are unknown.
checks: Read the balance sheet and cash flow statement: check borrowings, short-term debt, inventory and whether operating cash flow supports the reported profit.

Find out why the net margin has fallen for two years even as sales grew, for example input costs, exchange rates, pricing or competition. Check the latest quarterly results (quarter ended June 30, 2026) for the direction.

Read the Oct 1, 2026 'Material Information' notice and the corporate briefing for anything explaining the weak share price. Also check that the dividend is covered by earnings and cash, since only a short payout history is on record.

MEBL.summary: Meezan Bank scores 71.8/100 (HOLD), driven by strong multi-year growth in sales and EPS, rising margins, a 5.5% dividend yield and a share price that has beaten the KSE-100. The valuation looks expensive: the P/E of 10.3 is about 1.5x the sector median of 6.7. Three bank-specific factors (price-to-book, bad loans, capital adequacy) carry 38% of the weight and are unscored, and data coverage is only 62%, so the score is incomplete.
strengths: Sales grew about 26.5% a year and EPS about 25.4% a year over three years, with net margin up from 19.39% to 21.18%.
Cash dividends paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record, with a 5.5% yield and interim payouts rising from 70% to 80% of face value.
Price is above its 200-day average and has beaten the KSE-100 by about 19.5 points over roughly a year.
risks: Valuation is the weakest scored factor (36.9/100): the stock trades at a clear premium to other banks on P/E.

Latest annual figures show a step back: 2025 sales fell to Rs 285.1bn from Rs 315.9bn, profit to Rs 89.0bn from Rs 101.5bn, and EPS to Rs 49.54 from Rs 56.62. The strong 3-year growth rates are measured from a low 2022 base and hide this decline.
The scorecard cannot see asset quality (non-performing loans), capital adequacy or price-to-book, the main measures of a bank's safety and value. Debt, funding and cash flow details are also absent.
checks: Find the non-performing loan ratio and loan-loss provisioning in the latest annual report and the September 2026 quarterly report.
Check the capital adequacy ratio against the regulator's minimum, and the equity figure to work out price-to-book.
Read the reasons for the 2025 fall in profit and whether the nine-month 2026 results show recovery or further decline.

PAKT.summary: PAKT scores 71.7/100 (HOLD). The score rests on solid sales growth, a very high dividend yield (8.6%) and a mid-range valuation (P/E 10.8, in line with the sector median). Only 62% of the scorecard could be measured. Debt, cash flow and liquidity are all missing, so the score says nothing about balance sheet strength.
strengths: Sales grew about 13.6% a year over three years, from Rs 94.9bn in 2022 to Rs 139.0bn in 2025
Dividend yield of 8.6% scored 94.5, and cash dividends were paid in each fiscal year on record, with four cash payouts announced in 2026

risks: Net margin has slipped from 26.3% in 2023 to 21.5% in 2025. The 11.9% yearly EPS growth is flattered by the low 2022 base: EPS was Rs 113.35 in 2023 and Rs 116.85 in 2025, only about 3% higher in two years
The 8.6% yield on a Rs 1,495 price implies roughly Rs 128 a share in dividends, which is above 2025 EPS of Rs 116.85. If so, the payout may not be sustainable if profits don't grow

Debt, cash flow quality, cash conversion and liquidity are not scored (38% of the weight). The shares also lagged the KSE-100 by about 17 points over the past year. The sector P/E comparison may rest on very few peers, so 'in line with the sector' tells you little
checks: Look at the cash flow statement and balance sheet: is operating cash flow enough to cover dividends, and how much debt does the company carry?
Read the quarterly results for the period ended 30 September 2026 to see whether margins are still falling or have steadied
Compare dividends paid per share with EPS over several years, and ask what is driving the margin decline (costs, pricing, taxes or product mix)

GADT.summary: GADT scores 70.6 out of 100, mostly because it looks very cheap: a P/E of 2.7 against a sector median of 6.6 earns the maximum valuation score.
